method: Source-bound editorial name comparisons. Similar spellings do not prove the same person or same historical event. All eight cases are pending independent specialist review.

cases.title: Aššur and Asshur in Genesis
cases.question: Do similar names prove that a dated Assyrian archive and a Genesis passage record the same referent?
cases.finding: Middle Assyrian tablet catalogues locate documents at Aššur, while Genesis 10 contains biblical Asshur language. These witnesses have different genres, contexts and dates; the archive does not equate a named ancestor with a tablet findspot.
cases.limit: The similarity of these Romanised spellings alone is not an historical identity argument.
cases.next: Compare original Hebrew and Akkadian forms, textual transmission and securely dated geographical studies.

evidence.note: The catalogue supplies an Aššur archival context, not an identified biblical individual.
Genesis is primary for what this biblical text says, not for an excavation provenance.

cases.title: Nineveh in chronicle and prophecy
cases.question: Are a surviving Babylonian chronicle and biblical prophetic accounts interchangeable records?
cases.finding: The Babylonian Chronicle case and the prophecies in Nahum and Zephaniah name Nineveh. Their genres, composition histories and physical witnesses differ; the later copy date of the Chronicle is not the date of the event it recounts.
cases.limit: Shared naming alone does not establish identical details, motives or textual chronology.
cases.next: Independently review published chronicle lines, copy chronology and the literary contexts of both prophets.

evidence.note: This object is a later copy of an ancient chronicle about Nineveh.
Nahum explicitly introduces its prophetic subject as Nineveh.
Zephaniah supplies another distinct prophetic reference to the city.

cases.title: Šibaniba and Tell Billa
cases.question: What evidence currently supports using both names for this provincial archive context?
cases.finding: The cited Billa 30 tablet is attributed to an archive described using Šibaniba and Tell Billa. This is a documented catalogue association and not a comprehensive new archaeological identification.
cases.limit: A single catalogue association cannot establish precise ancient borders, full site chronology or every variant spelling.
cases.next: Review excavation reports, findspot records, dating and historical-geographical treatments.

evidence.note: The tablet case provides the existing attributed provincial archive context.

cases.title: Niri-šaldi in a damaged line
cases.question: Can a partly damaged personal name be matched to a second person or document?
cases.finding: The credited editor records the name in a particular obverse line of a Middle Assyrian footwear account. The archive preserves this edition-scoped reading without constructing an unsupported biography.
cases.limit: Damage and a single local attestation do not justify a broader person identification.
cases.next: Obtain qualified collation of the damaged signs and examine independently edited parallel attestations.

evidence.note: The named recipient occurs in the editor's cited damaged tablet line.

cases.title: Sargon in Isaiah 20
cases.question: What supports this ruler's identification in the existing local concordance?
cases.finding: Isaiah 20 directly names Sargon in its narrative. The concordance entry does not yet attach a specific independently edited royal-inscription line or identified physical artefact.
cases.limit: A missing object-level link in this index says nothing about the wider existence of historical Sargon inscriptions.
cases.next: Add an independently identified royal inscription, edition citation, line number and specialist translation assessment.

evidence.note: Isaiah is the cited biblical witness, distinct from an Assyrian inscription.

cases.title: Hezekiah in Second Kings
cases.question: Does the biblical account by itself establish a line-by-line match to an Assyrian royal inscription?
cases.finding: Second Kings 18 supplies the named ruler and a biblical account of conflict. No separately identified Assyrian object and edition line is attached to this specific concordance entry.
cases.limit: Different documents require textual and chronological comparison, not an assumed word-for-word match.
cases.next: Add identified royal edition lines with stated dating, translation uncertainty and independent historical review.

evidence.note: The referenced verses are the present biblical source for this entry.

cases.title: Jehu in Second Kings
cases.question: Can name similarity alone identify the biblical Jehu with an object from another source?
cases.finding: Second Kings 9 provides the indexed narrative for Jehu of Israel. The term currently lacks an independently specified archaeological line or object association in this concordance.
cases.limit: The missing link is a limitation of this local index, not a claim that no relevant external material exists.
cases.next: Examine authenticated object editions and historical chronology before publishing a direct identification.

evidence.note: This is the cited biblical passage, without a separate local object claim.

cases.title: Samaria and multiple biblical reports
cases.question: Which distinct events and passages currently support the use of Samaria as a historical place name?
cases.finding: Second Kings 17 contains separate references to Samaria, the siege narrative and later resettlement. The current concordance has no specified Assyrian tablet or object line for this place entry.
cases.limit: Separate episodes must not be compressed into one event or used to infer unmeasured city extent and population.
cases.next: Compare dated Assyrian inscriptions and verified site evidence against the precise biblical passages.

evidence.note: This narrative concerns Samaria and its political crisis.
This separate passage describes resettlement as recorded in Kings.
